Acute

/uh-KYOOT/ — rhymes with 'a flute' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Acute is felt or experienced to an intense, sharp degree.

He felt acute embarrassment when his phone rang loudly during the silent exam.

Worked Example

Halfway up the trail, Priya's ankle twisted on a loose rock. The pain was so sharp and overwhelming that she couldn't take another step, and her friends had to help her back down the mountain.

Priya's pain was acute — experienced at an intense, piercing degree. 'Mild' discomfort lets you keep hiking; acute pain stops you cold.

How Acute Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

intense

intense: existing in a very strong degree

severe

piercing: sharp enough to cut through

Antonyms

mild

mild: gentle and not strong

dull

dull: weak, blunted, not sharp

How Strong Is It? — noticeable → acute → excruciating

noticeable vs. acute

noticeable vs. acute: Noticeable is weaker than acute — a noticeable feeling registers, but an acute one dominates everything else you sense.

excruciating vs. acute

excruciating vs. acute: Excruciating is stronger than acute — acute pain is intense, but excruciating pain is unbearable torture.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — acu-

root — acu-: needle, sharp point (Latin)

suffix — -te (-tus)

suffix — -te (-tus): having been made so (participle ending) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin acuere meant 'to sharpen.' Something acute has been 'sharpened to a point' — pain, senses, or a crisis felt at needle-sharp intensity.

Use the root in a new word: acupuncture

Use the root in a new word: acupuncture: Acupuncture treats pain by placing fine needles at precise points on the body.

Word Choice

Often pairs with pain, shortage, crisis, or senses (acute hearing); in medicine, acute means sudden and severe, the opposite of long-lasting chronic conditions.
